nodes.question: Which Sustainable Development Goal is particularly at risk due to the impacts of climate change?
nodes.answer: Sustainable Development Goal 8, which focuses on sustained, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth and employment, is particularly at risk due to the impacts of climate change.
nodes.paragraph: The review identifies several avenues for future research and highlights specific features and trade-offs relevant to policymakers interested in enabling the banking system to contribute to sustained economic development in the face of worsening physical climate risks. Keywords Banking Climate change Economic resilience Financial institutions Financial stability Natural hazards JEL Classification E51 G21 010 Q54 * Vinzenz Peters vinzenz.peters@maastrichtuniversity.nl 1 Maastricht University, Maastricht, Netherlands 48 V. Peters 1 Introduction Natural hazard shocks (such as disasters, extreme weather events, and climate shocks) pose significant threats to economic growth and employment in affected regions (Botzen et al., 2019; Klomp & Valckx, 2014). With progressing climate change, such events are expected to become more frequent and severe in large parts of the world (e.g., Hoeppe, 2016; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2022). Policymakers and scientists continuously express their concerns that the physical and societal consequences of a warming climate and natural hazard shocks threaten progress in human development, as codified in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through the destruction of capital, the disruption of business, and the loss of human livelihoods, the goal of sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth and employment (SDG 8) is particularly at risk (World Economic Forum, 2023; World Meteorological Organization, 2023).

nodes.question: What methodological differences impact the econometric estimation of household welfare effects in the studies?
nodes.answer: Differences impact the treatment of extreme weather variables, modeling of standard errors, and the inclusion of appropriate control variables.
nodes.paragraph: 2020 ; Sam et al. 2021 ). The impact of climate-induced weather events on household welfare at the micro-level has been the subject of an overwhelming number of studies in the literature.3 Even though these studies provide valuable insights into the extent to which households are affected, carrying out proper cross-study comparisons and drawing definitive conclusions regarding the quantitative impact on welfare is challenging owing to their use of different types of data and methodologies. For example, from a data perspective, there are differences in how studies measure the occurrence of an extreme event, whether by simply indicating the event incidence, deriving climate and asset-based damage functions, or using ex-post damage assessments (Kumar et al. 2023 ; Nguyen et al. 2023). From a methodological viewpoint, there is also variation in how studies econometrically estimate the impact on household wel - fare, including their treatment of extreme weather variables, modeling of standard errors, and the inclusion of appropriate control variables (Hsiang 2016 ; Berlemann and Tran 2020 ; Albertini et al. 2022 ). The purpose of this paper is to present a common framework in terms of (i) geo-spatial modeling the damages due to extreme climate events, and (ii) the use of damage proxies and subsequent challenges in terms of obtaining quantitative estimates through econometric tools and data type.

On the other hand, economywide models have proven valuable for capturing economic impacts across sectors using destruction coefficients and supply shocks (Bosello et al. 2007 ; Liu et al. 2020 ; Wu and Guo, 2021 ). Previous applications of this type of studies, mainly on a global scale, analyze the repercussions of climatic shocks on the economy and livelihoods (Bosello et al. 2007 ; Darwin and Tol 2001 ; Deke et al. 2001 ), as well as food security (Golub et al. 2013 ; Pe a-L vano et al. 2019 ). Nevertheless, only a few studies focus on specific countries and conduct in-depth analysis using single-country models. In this study, we build a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model for Nigeria to examine the socio-economic and food security impacts of climate disasters in detail. Recent CGE studies have analyze events such as floods (Avelino and Dall erba, 2019 ), droughts (Wittwer and Griffith 2011 ), and cyclones (Washida et al. 2014 ), identifying two key transmission channels: reduced productive capacity and increased prices.

nodes.question: Which sectors are particularly highlighted as vulnerable to exogenous shocks?
nodes.answer: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and otherwise underserved and excluded populations are particularly vulnerable.
nodes.paragraph: Limiting the negative economic consequences of future natural hazard shocks is therefore an urgent and high-priority policy goal (Koubi, 2019; United Nations, 2015). It is widely acknowledged that the banking sector has an important role to play in this endeavour (Carney, 2015; Ranger et al., 2021; United Nations, 2023). By facilitating access to finance, banks can enhance economic resilience through critical times and contribute to sustained economic growth and employment participation across societal groups. This is particularly true for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and otherwise underserved and excluded populations, which are highly vulnerable to exogenous shocks. However, the relationship between natural hazards, banks, and real economic resilience is more complex than this. First, banks themselves can be negatively impacted and experience losses and threats to their financial health, potentially limiting the ability to supply recovery loans. Second, banks may differ in their willingness to support economic recovery based on their business models, ownership structures, and resulting objective functions (Beck et al., 2018; Brei & Schclarek, 2015).
